chunks.chunk_text:
The durable unit of knowledge work is becoming the human + agent + corpus assemblage. The human sets intent, taste, exception judgment, and accountability. The agent performs bounded cognitive labor: search, draft, reconcile, test, summarize, route, and monitor. The corpus supplies memory, source provenance, permissions, canonical language, and institutional constraint. This matters because the model alone is not the firm. Microsoft frames the frontier firm around intelligence on tap and human-agent teams. OpenAI enterprise telemetry shows workers using AI across repeatable multi-step work. Anthropic usage data shows experience effects: high-tenure users attempt higher-value tasks and elicit more successful responses. The strategic change is not that every worker has a chatbot. It is that work can be decomposed into human-owned intent, agent-executed tasks, and corpus-grounded evidence loops. The firm that understands this will not ask, "How do we make the analyst faster?" It will ask, "Which assemblage owns this decision, what sources can it use, what actions can it take, and where must a human intervene?" Claim summary: Knowledge-work productivity shifts from individual output to a governed assemblage of human judgment, bounded agents, and a source-grounded corpus. AbarVa framing: AbarVa treats this as a context-layer problem: corpus quality, tenant binding, graph relationships, and agent doctrine determine whether AI becomes useful enterprise infrastructure. Evidence basis: verified public research and company source material. The point is not that any single source proves the thesis. The pattern matters because independent evidence now points in the same direction: models are getting better at task execution, enterprise buyers are reorganizing around AI, and the missing layer is governed context rather than generic fluency. So what: CIOs should fund the context layer before broad automation. Investors should value binding-layer control points. In industrial work, the factory floor determined what could be produced repeatedly. In knowledge work, the corpus now plays that role. A useful corpus is not a document dump. It is the structured, permissioned, versioned substrate of the firm's memory: policies, decisions, customer context, product truth, source evidence, playbooks, metrics, exceptions, and prior outcomes. Retrieval-augmented generation showed why external knowledge matters for knowledge-intensive generation. But long-context research shows that more context alone is not enough; models can fail to use information robustly when relevant material sits in the middle of long inputs. The strategic implication is simple: corpus work is operations work. Teams need source hygiene, chunking discipline, metadata, recency rules, evidence ledgers, conflict resolution, and permission boundaries. The firm with the best corpus does not merely answer questions faster. It makes better delegation possible because agents can work against trusted institutional memory rather than guessing from parametric priors. The word agent invites overreach. A useful enterprise agent should be treated less like a synthetic employee and more like a bounded worker in a process design. It has a job, permitted tools, accessible sources, success criteria, stop conditions, logging, and escalation rules. Anthropic's engineering guidance is a useful corrective: workflows are better where tasks are predictable and consistency matters; agents are appropriate where flexible model-driven decisions are required. If it removes the first rung, it will later ask why nobody has second-rung judgment. The assemblage must make expertise more teachable, not merely labor cheaper. The winning firm will not be the one with the most prompts. It will be the one whose assemblages learn. Every completed workflow should leave residue: better source chunks, sharper task templates, clearer exceptions, improved evaluation sets, updated permissions, known failure cases, stronger acceptance criteria, and reusable decisions. Anthropic's learning-curve evidence suggests experienced users become better at harnessing models. Microsoft points toward context, observability, and governed agent operations. NIST and ISO show that management systems must improve over time, not merely approve initial use. RAG shows why external memory matters; corpus discipline makes that memory reusable. This is the compounding loop: humans set intent, agents execute bounded work, the corpus grounds and records it, governance audits it, outcomes measure it, and the next task starts from a better base. That is the future of knowledge work: not humans versus agents, but accountable people commanding systems that remember.
